newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - Vietnam struggles with the information age.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Vietnam struggles with the information age.

text.p: Before playing to an ecstatic crowd in Ho Chi Minh City last month, British rock star Sting had to submit a translation of his lyrics to Vietnam's Ministry of Culture and Information for approval.
Sting may have been surprised. But the demand raised few eyebrows in a country where control of information and censorship against foreign cultural "pollution" have long been a way of life.

In the last decade Vietnam has opened its doors to overseas investors. But the lessons of a hard-fought independence have not been forsaken, as a harsh purge of foreign cultural influences and goods underlined earlier this year.

But now, with the advent of Internet, policy-makers are faced with the dilemma of how to erect a "bamboo curtain" in cyberspace and, at the same time, live up to their promise of taking the country into the information age.

In 1995, the government adopted a resolution, reported to require investment of up to $500 million, declaring that by the end of the century information technology would become "one of the spearheads of the country", with software development a priority.
By most measures, the plan has so far been a failure.

Michel Dauget, managing director of Pacific R.I.M., Vietnam's first foreign software venture, says that "with cheap labour and talented workers, there is great potential for inexpensive, high quality software development here."
"But it won't happen until Vietnam has the Internet," he says.
To the majority in Vietnam, one of the world's poorest countries, the Internet remains off limits.
There are only an estimated 100,000 computers nationwide, many of which are in the offices of foreign companies.
But enthusiasm for cyberspace is already running high.

Despite the absence of a full-access Internet node, a handful of limited service providers has sprouted from various government offices. The best of these offer international e-mail, albeit typically with an "official" delay, and "Intranet" with Web pages available only inside Vietnam.

The numbers are paltry in comparison to the real Internet -- several thousand subscribers and a dozen or so Web pages. With so many service providers for so few users, competition is keen, each hoping to cash in when the government opens the door.
FULL INTERNET SERVICE POSSIBLE SHORTLY
According to industry insiders, that may happen very soon.

"I think maybe this month or next the government will allow us to provide full Internet service," says Nguyen Anh Tuan, managing director of Teltic, a service provider and subsidiary of the national telecom authority.
Perhaps the most troubling aspect for Hanoi are the millions of Vietnamese who have fled the country since the communist victory in 1975.
Years later, some of them still have an axe to grind.
Hien Do Ky, who is now an engineer in Canada, left in 1980. His father, a civil servant at the telecom office in former South Vietnam, was jailed for five years when the war ended.
Sixteen years on, Hien has strong feelings about the government, which in his view is trying to consolidate its power and refusing to talk about political reform.
"The government does not have popular support from its citizens," he says. "It must keep its people in the dark and under surveillance to survive".
To counter this, Hien uses the Internet to gather and disseminate information which he hopes will one day help establish a new political landscape in his homeland.
He is just one individual. More menacing for Hanoi are the organised groups of dissidents and activists, which by one estimate number 130.
The National United Front for the Liberation of Vietnam, for example, aims to "shed light on Vietnam's situation behind Hanoi's propaganda" through its Vinsight Web page.

Another group says it has already got behind the "bamboo curtain" by sending e-mail through existing networks. And an international human rights group has reported incidents of overseas Vietnamese "spamming" -- clogging up with a barrage of e-mail -- Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet's account.
With full Internet access raising the spectre of dissident voices being heard nationwide, why would Hanoi even tinker with the idea?
Handicapped in recent decades by war, geo-politics and central planning, the country is loathe to slip further behind.
ONLY ASEAN COUNTRY NOT ON INTERNET

Vietnam is now the only member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) not connected to Internet. Singapore, often seen as a cultural mentor for Hanoi, is becoming an "information hub" and China, an old rival but ideological ally, is hooked up. Even the local press has criticised the government's foot dragging.
Despite its dark side, opening up to cyberspace is seen as inevitable.

Internet regulations are not yet final, though some of the principles are already clear. The government will eavesdrop on the network and erect a firewall probably similar to Singapore's. Subscribers will be held responsible for content, both transmitted and received, and service providers are all likely to be state-owned.
In a measure that promotes heavy screening, service providers' licences may be revoked and their equipment confiscated if subscribers are caught sending offensive or subversive material.
The goal of this, according to John Barnes, an adviser at Hung Vuong Computer, is "to cast the net so wide that in the event there's a problem no one will escape".
Others are not so sure.
As one Western industry executive put it, when the volume of traffic hits a critical mass, controlling cyberspace will be like grasping a slippery fish.
